name: Erakeswara Temple, Pillalamarri
deity: Shiva, worshipped as Erakeswara, in one of the four old stone temples of Pillalamarri.
dynasty: Kakatiya, built by the Recherla family, their feudatories
summary: Erakeswara Temple at Pillalamarri, built about 1208 CE by a lady of the Recherla chiefs, is one of the finely carved Shiva temples of a village that was once their seat of power.

sections.history: Pillalamarri, just outside Suryapet, was a seat of the Recherla chiefs, who served the Kakatiya kings as feudatories. The Erakeswara Temple is dated to about 1208 CE and is associated with Erakasani, the wife of the Recherla chief Beti Reddi, who is remembered as its patron. It stands in a group of four old stone temples in the village, from the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, which includes the Nameswara Temple of about 1202, raised by Namireddi on the bank of the Musi river, and a Trikuteswara shrine, the "lord of three shrines". The group is admired for its carved stonework, and Pillalamarri is one of the few places where the artistry of the Recherla court, which also produced Ramappa, can be seen at close hand.
sections.architecture: Erakeswara is a stone temple in the Kakatiya manner, standing in a village setting among its sister temples. The Shiva sanctum and its hall show the finish for which the Kakatiya sculptors are known, with carved pillars, doorways and eaves worked with careful detail. As in other Kakatiya temples, the design is a measured composition of sanctum, hall and porch rather than a towering monument. Compared with the great temples of Warangal, it is modest in scale, and its charm lies in the quality of its carving and its setting among neighbouring shrines of the same age.
sections.legends: Erakeswara is known more through its patronage than through a famous legend. The temple is linked to Erakasani, a woman of the Recherla family, whose gift of a Shiva temple stands as an example of women's patronage in the Kakatiya country. Local tradition honours the group of four temples as a single sacred precinct of the Recherla chiefs, who also stood behind the Ramappa Temple, and speaks of Pillalamarri as a place where their devotion to Shiva took its most refined stone form.
sections.festivals: Shiva worship in the Telugu country is marked by Maha Shivaratri, observed in February or March, by Mondays, and by the month of Karthika in the autumn, and local devotees may gather at the Pillalamarri temples on such days. Confirm any observances and dates locally.
sections.experience: Pillalamarri is a quiet, rewarding stop for those who enjoy the carved detail of Kakatiya stonework. Because the four old temples lie close together, a visit can take in the Erakeswara, Nameswara and Trikuteswara shrines in a single unhurried walk. The setting is a working village, so expect a peaceful and local atmosphere rather than crowds. It pairs naturally with Ramappa, Kota Gullu and the Warangal monuments, though it lies at some distance from them, near Suryapet on the road between Hyderabad and Vijayawada.

visit.timings: The temple is a place of worship and a protected heritage site, and opening hours are not fixed. Please confirm timings and access locally before travelling, and plan a daylight visit.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is appreciated, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is removed at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography of the exterior and carvings is generally acceptable; follow any posted rules and the instructions of temple staff, and avoid photographing worship without permission.
visit.gettingThere: Pillalamarri lies just outside Suryapet town in Suryapet district, on the Hyderabad–Vijayawada highway. Suryapet has rail and bus services, Hyderabad is the nearest major airport, and the temples are reached by road from Suryapet.
